Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals What is Face Milling: Process, tools and operation Published Jun 13, 2025, updated Jun 19, 2025 7 min Table of Contents What Is Face Milling? How the Face Milling Process Works Common Face Milling Tools Types of Face Milling Operations Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling doesn’t get the spotlight much, but it’s one of those workhorse processes that keeps machining shops running smooth. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Face Milling Operations Summary Operation Type Description When to Use Conventional Face Milling Full-width surface passes General surface flattening Partial Face Milling Only part of cutter contacts surface Smaller or irregular workpieces Climb Milling Cutter feeds with the work Best for finish (requires stable setup) Conventional Milling Cutter moves against feed Safer on older or flexible machines Slotting / Contour Facing Shallow pockets or curved surfaces Non-flat geometries, careful setups Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling ( reddit ) You can have the best tools on the shelf, but if you don’t dial in your technique, the finish will show it. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. Tool Geometry Cheat Sheet: Choosing the Right Insert Material Recommended Geometry Rake Angle Notes Mild Steel Positive rake, round tip +10° to +20° Reduces cutting force, good surface finish Aluminum Sharp edge, polished +20° or more Prevents built-up edge, clean finish Stainless Steel Honed edge, tough grade 0° to +10° Needs stronger insert, avoid sharp corners Cast Iron Negative rake, strong edge 0° or negative Stable cut, handles interrupted surfaces Titanium Positive rake, low feed +10° Reduce heat, avoid rubbing Choosing the wrong insert isn't just a waste of money, it'll eat your surface finish alive Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling is one of those processes that rewards the prepared. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. And if you’d rather not deal with tool geometry, chip clearance, or babysitting a facing milling machine , we’ve got your back. JLCCNC handles everything from single prototypes to high-volume runs, so you can skip the trial-and-error and get perfect surfaces from day one. Not sure if CNC milling is even the right choice for your part? Check out our comparison of CNC machining vs sheet metal fabrication to make the right call before you commit. How the Face Milling Process Works Common Face Milling Tools Types of Face Milling Operations Best Practices for Cleaner Face Milling Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling doesn’t get the spotlight much, but it’s one of those workhorse processes that keeps machining shops running smooth. If you’ve ever needed a flat surface that’s actually flat , you’ve relied on it, whether you realized it or not. So what exactly is face milling? Think of it as the process behind every perfectly squared metal block, every smooth aluminum plate, every clean surface that just feels right. It’s precise, fast, and oddly satisfying to watch. But it’s not just about spinning a tool across some metal. The cutter design, tool path, speeds, and setup all play a role in getting that crisp finish without wrecking your inserts or your workpiece. In this guide, we’re breaking down how face milling works, what tools you’ll need, the types of operations involved, and a few tips that’ll save your cutters, and your sanity. What Is Face Milling? (istock) Face milling is one of the most common, and most essential, processes in the machining world. It’s all about cutting a flat surface perpendicular to the tool’s axis, usually with a wide face mill cutter that skims across the top of the material. The result? A smooth, level finish that’s ready for the next operation. Unlike side milling , which cuts along the edge or profile of a part, face milling focuses on creating a clean, wide face. It’s often the first step in squaring up a workpiece or prepping raw stock in a facing milling machine . What makes it effective is the tool design. A face mill tool typically uses multiple cutting edges (inserts) mounted in a circular holder. These inserts do most of the work, shaving off material in fast, controlled passes. You’ll find face mills in CNC shops, manual mills, and production floors alike, especially where consistency and finish quality matter. How the Face Milling Process Works The concept is simple: a rotating face mill sweeps across the surface of your material, cutting with the edges on the bottom of the tool. The setup, however, is where the real work begins. In a typical operation, the facing mill is mounted in a vertical spindle. As it spins, the inserts take shallow bites out of the material with each pass. The machine feeds the workpiece horizontally while the tool keeps cutting, layer by layer. It’s fast, consistent, and perfect for prepping a surface for tight-tolerance parts. The results depend on your setup, feed rate, cutting speed, tool path, and depth of cut all play a role. A roughing pass might take off more material quickly, while a finishing pass uses a finer face milling cutter for that clean, reflective finish. Tool rigidity and part stability matter. If your setup flexes, the finish suffers. If your inserts are dull, you’ll get chatter and uneven cuts. It's the kind of job where details make all the difference, and a decent face milling machine won't cover for poor planning. Roughing vs Finishing Parameter Roughing Finishing Depth of Cut 2–5 mm (0.08–0.2 in) 0.2–1 mm (0.01–0.04 in) Feed Rate Higher (aggressive) Lower (controlled) Cutting Speed Moderate Higher Tool Used Indexable face mill Fly cutter / fine-tooth mill Surface Finish Coarse Smooth (low Ra value) Common Face Milling Tools There’s more than one way to flatten a surface, and the tool you pick makes a big difference on your finish, your cycle time, and your tooling cost. Let’s break down the most common options used in face milling . Tool Selection Guide: When to Use What Tool Type Best For Pros Cons Face Mill Cutter General purpose, roughing + finishing Fast, efficient, easy insert swap Higher upfront cost Shell Mill Large parts, modular setups Versatile, scalable Needs arbor and holder setup Fly Cutter Finishing small to medium surfaces Inexpensive, smooth finish Slow, can vibrate at high speeds Solid Carbide Tool Light machines, tight spaces Rigid, compact Pricey, limited insert options Types of Face Milling Operations (ResearchGate) Face milling isn’t just about plowing a tool across a block of metal. There are different ways to run the cut, and knowing the options helps you get better results, or avoid screwing things up. Conventional Face Milling This is your go-to method. The face mill cuts across the entire top of the workpiece, removing material in overlapping passes. It’s efficient and ideal for prepping flat surfaces quickly. Partial Face Milling When the workpiece is smaller or has tricky geometry, only part of the face milling cutter engages with the material. It requires a bit more care in setup to avoid deflection and uneven cuts. Climb vs. Conventional Milling In climb milling, the cutter moves in the same direction as the feed, great finish, but it needs a solid machine. Conventional milling moves against the feed direction and offers more stability for older or lightweight machines. Some facing milling machines allow switching between the two. Slotting and Contour Facing Not every job is a square block. Face mills can be used for shallow slots or contoured faces if the toolpath is planned right. Just don’t expect perfect results unless your setup is rock solid. Here’s what separates clean cuts from chewed-up messes. ● Keep your toolpath smooth—avoid sharp corners or direction changes mid-cut. ● Use coolant when possible. It extends insert life and keeps chips out of the way. ● Watch your depth of cut—too deep and you’ll get chatter, too shallow and the tool may rub instead of cut. ● Rigid setup matters more than fancy tooling. If your part moves, your surface finish suffers. And finally, picking the right tool geometry matters. The insert’s shape, rake, and edge prep can make or break your finish, especially on tricky materials. Tool Geometry Cheat Sheet: Choosing the Right Insert Material Recommended Geometry Rake Angle Notes Mild Steel Positive rake, round tip +10° to +20° Reduces cutting force, good surface finish Aluminum Sharp edge, polished +20° or more Prevents built-up edge, clean finish Stainless Steel Honed edge, tough grade 0° to +10° Needs stronger insert, avoid sharp corners Cast Iron Negative rake, strong edge 0° or negative Stable cut, handles interrupted surfaces Titanium Positive rake, low feed +10° Reduce heat, avoid rubbing Choosing the wrong insert isn't just a waste of money, it'll eat your surface finish alive Master the Cut Before You Hit Cycle Start Face milling is one of those processes that rewards the prepared. The right face mill tool , a solid setup, and a bit of know-how can take your surface finish from “rough passable” to production-ready. And if you’d rather not deal with tool geometry, chip clearance, or babysitting a facing milling machine , we’ve got your back. Manufacturing Services Blog Blog Home Blog Knowledge Hub CNC Machining Fundamentals Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: A Guide to Choosing the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Published Jan 27, 2024, updated Oct 15, 2026 18 min Table of Contents The Core Difference CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Decision Framework How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree Where Sheet Metal Wins Where CNC Machining Wins Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal One Hybrid Assembly Example Material Considerations The Real Cost Curve A Common Mistake Worth Flagging FAQ Not Sure Which Process Fits Your Part? Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Need CNC and Sheet Metal? We've Got Both JLCCNC does both CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication in-house. Upload your file, get an instant quote. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. A Common Mistake Worth Flagging Choosing a process based on which one a designer is more familiar with, rather than which one actually fits the part, is a frequent and costly habit. An engineer used to specifying machined parts sometimes defaults to CNC even for a simple bent bracket that sheet metal would produce at a fraction of the cost — not from any real requirement, just familiarity. Running through the decision factors and the 5-step tree above explicitly, rather than defaulting to habit, is a genuinely cheap way to avoid overpaying on a part that didn't need machining's capability in the first place. FAQ Is sheet metal fabrication always cheaper than CNC machining? Not always — at very low volume the two can be close, and for parts needing tight tolerances or complex 3D geometry, machining is often the only option regardless of cost. Sheet metal's cost advantage grows most clearly at moderate-to-high volume for parts within its geometric capability. Can a part be redesigned to use sheet metal instead of machining to save cost? Often, yes — if the part's function doesn't actually require variable thickness or fine 3D features, redesigning around uniform-thickness formed geometry can meaningfully cut cost, especially at volume. This is worth evaluating during design review rather than after tooling or a first production run. What tolerance can sheet metal fabrication achieve? Typical sheet metal tolerances run around ±0.1–0.3mm depending on the process and material thickness — tighter than many people assume, but still generally looser than CNC machining's ±0.01–0.05mm capability. Which process has a faster lead time? It depends on where you are in the product cycle. For a single prototype, CNC machining often turns around faster since there's no tooling or bend planning involved. Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Need CNC and Sheet Metal? We've Got Both JLCCNC does both CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication in-house. Upload your file, get an instant quote. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. A Common Mistake Worth Flagging Choosing a process based on which one a designer is more familiar with, rather than which one actually fits the part, is a frequent and costly habit. An engineer used to specifying machined parts sometimes defaults to CNC even for a simple bent bracket that sheet metal would produce at a fraction of the cost — not from any real requirement, just familiarity. Running through the decision factors and the 5-step tree above explicitly, rather than defaulting to habit, is a genuinely cheap way to avoid overpaying on a part that didn't need machining's capability in the first place. Applications of CNC Lathes FAQ (AI-generated) CNC lathes remain one of the most important machine types in modern manufacturing, powering industries from automotive to aerospace with accuracy, speed, and repeatability. If you're researching CNC lathing for your next project—or comparing CNC lathe machines, CNC machine lathes, or even trying to understand what is a CNC lathe —this guide gives you everything you need to make informed decisions. And if you're looking for fast, reliable machining services, JLCCNC provides high-precision CNC turning and milling with instant quoting and a wide selection of materials to support both prototyping and production. Understanding CNC Lathes Definition and Key Components of a CNC Lathe A CNC lathe is a computer-controlled machine tool designed to rotate a workpiece while cutting tools remove material to create cylindrical or conical geometries. Unlike manual lathes, CNC lathe machines operate through programmed commands, ensuring consistent dimensions even across large production batches. A typical CNC lathe machine includes: Headstock : houses the spindle that rotates the part Chuck : grips the material Tool turret : holds multiple CNC tools Bed & carriage : provide machine rigidity Control system : executes CNC turning programs Tailstock (optional): supports long workpieces These elements work together to deliver smooth, accurate cutting, making CNC lathing suitable for both simple shafts and highly complex components. Differences Between CNC Lathes and Conventional Lathes Conventional lathes require manual adjustments, which slows down production and introduces human error. A CNC machine lathe, by contrast, runs automated toolpaths defined in G-code. The benefits include: Faster cycle times Higher precision and repeatability Better safety Ability to handle complex geometries Automated multi-tool operations For manufacturers needing accuracy within microns or consistent production day after day, CNC lathes outperform manual machines in every category. Core Advantages of CNC Lathing CNC lathing offers several strong advantages: Superior roundness and concentricity for rotational parts Excellent surface finish due to continuous cutting Strong material compatibility , including aluminum, steel, stainless steel, copper, brass, plastics, and more Great scalability , from prototypes to mass production Tight tolerances , often ±0.005 mm on high-end systems These strengths explain why CNC lathe machines remain foundational in nearly all manufacturing sectors. How CNC Lathe Machines Work (AI-generated) Overview of the Lathing Process The CNC lathing process begins by mounting raw material—typically a bar or billet—into the chuck. As the spindle rotates the workpiece, CNC cutting tools move linearly along X and Z axes to remove material and create the desired geometry. CNC lathing is especially efficient for: Shafts Pins Bushings Sleeves Threads Custom cylindrical forms Because the workpiece rotates while the tool moves, the process is optimized for parts where diameter features dominate. CNC Programming Basics for Turning Operations At the heart of every CNC lathe machine is a program composed of G-code and M-code . These commands tell the machine: How fast to the spindle rotate How quickly do cutting tools feed into the material Which tools to activate What path should the tool follow Programs are often written manually for simple parts or generated with CAD/CAM software for complex geometries. Understanding these fundamentals is essential for efficient CNC lathing. Motion Control and Spindle Operation CNC lathes synchronize motion between the spindle and cutting tools. Toolpaths rely on precise feed rates, calculated surface speeds, and appropriate depth of cut. Advanced CNC machine lathes use: Servo motors for precise tool motion Variable-frequency drives to control spindle speed Automatic tool changers for seamless multi-operation machining Together, these systems deliver both speed and accuracy. Common Types of CNC Lathe Machines Horizontal CNC Lathes Horizontal CNC lathes are the most widely used type of turning equipment, with the spindle oriented parallel to the machine bed. They excel at machining long, cylindrical parts and support both small-batch and mass production. Because chips naturally fall away from the cutting zone, these machines offer excellent chip evacuation, stable cutting conditions, and flexible turret configurations. Sizes range from compact turning centers—ideal for small parts—to heavy-duty industrial lathes capable of handling workpieces hundreds of millimeters in diameter. Many horizontal machines can be equipped with bar feeders, automatic loading systems, and sub-spindles to improve throughput. Key factors to evaluate include bed rigidity, spindle torque and speed, turret capacity, and the maximum turning diameter/length ratio (L/D), which influences stability and machining efficiency. Typical applications: shafts, bearing housings, cylinders, gear blanks, and various rotational components. Vertical CNC Lathes Vertical CNC lathes position the spindle vertically, with the workpiece mounted on a horizontal table. This configuration is ideal for large-diameter, short-height components, as gravity assists with part positioning and workholding stability. It also makes loading heavy parts safer and easier. Vertical lathes are known for exceptional rigidity when handling large, heavy, or wide workpieces, making them a staple in industries requiring oversized components. Important considerations include maximum turning diameter, table load capacity, machine rigidity, and spindle power. Typical applications: large flanges, disks, turbine housings, rotors, and components for wind power, construction, and heavy machinery. Precision CNC Lathes and Multi-Axis Machines Precision CNC lathes and multi-axis turning centers are designed for complex geometries and ultra-tight tolerances. These machines often include high-precision linear guides, thermal compensation systems, scale feedback, and advanced CNC controls. Multi-axis machines may integrate C-axis, Y-axis, sub-spindles, and driven tooling, allowing complete machining—turning, milling, drilling, and tapping—in a single setup. This reduces cycle time, improves accuracy, and eliminates secondary operations. Precision machines commonly use high-speed, low-vibration spindles and rigid tooling systems (such as HSK or BT holders) to deliver micron-level accuracy and excellent surface finishes. Typical applications: medical implants, aerospace components, precision instrument parts, high-end mold components, and any part requiring complex profiles or tight tolerances. CNC Lathe vs Other CNC Machines Key differences between CNC lathes and mills A CNC lathe operates by rotating the workpiece at high speed while the cutting tool remains stationary or moves along a controlled axis. This turning-based process makes it exceptionally effective for producing round, tubular, and symmetrical shapes with consistent concentricity. CNC mills, on the other hand, remove material using a rotating cutting tool that moves across multiple axes. Milling machines are better suited for flat surfaces, slots, pockets, and complex 3D forms. Compared with milling, a CNC lathe generally delivers higher efficiency for rotational components, faster material removal for cylindrical profiles, and tighter geometric tolerances for features such as diameters, tapers, and threads. If you're interested in understanding milling processes in more depth, you can continue with our Bed Milling Explained . Advantages of using a lathe for specific parts When manufacturing shafts, bushings, pins, spacers, and threaded connectors, a CNC lathe offers superior stability and repeatability. The continuous rotation of the workpiece allows for smooth surface finishes and accurate dimensional control, especially on long or slender parts. For high-volume production, the turning process significantly reduces cycle time, lowering overall machining costs. Modern CNC lathes can also integrate operations such as drilling, tapping, grooving, and parting directly into the same setup, minimizing repositioning errors. This combined functionality is highly beneficial for parts that require multiple machining steps but must maintain tight tolerance alignment across all features. Application scenarios A CNC lathe is widely applied across automotive, aerospace, medical devices, consumer electronics, industrial automation, and custom hardware manufacturing. Common examples include motor shafts, gear blanks, threaded inserts, precision fasteners, hydraulic fittings, valve components, connector housings, bearing parts, and high-accuracy prototypes. It is especially valuable in scenarios where roundness, diameter precision, and concentricity are critical. In prototyping, a CNC lathe supports quick iteration with consistent dimensional results, while in mass production, it ensures stable quality with efficient material utilization and reduced machining time. How Much Does a CNC Lathe Cost? Factors Affecting CNC Lathe Pricing CNC lathe machine cost varies widely. Key pricing factors include: Machine size and rigidity Horizontal vs vertical configuration Precision and number of axes Control system brand Maximum spindle speed Tool turret capacity Production-grade CNC lathes typically cost more because they offer tighter tolerances and faster cycle times. Typical Cost Ranges Approximate global pricing: Entry-level CNC lathes : $6,000–$15,000 Mid-range industrial machines : $20,000–$80,000 High-end multi-axis lathes : $100,000–$350,000+ Operational costs—tooling, maintenance, power—should also be considered. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for ProtoFlow PCBWay Plug-In for ProtoFlow by: PCBWay Oct 20,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News ProtoFlow is an AI-assisted PCB design tool for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It brings schematic capture, PCB layout and routing, and manufacturing file exports into one workspace. Users can describe a circuit in plain language to generate an editable schematic, then review, refine, and simulate the design. ProtoFlow also supports importing from and exporting to major EDA tools. Here is the link to ProtoFlow: https://www.protoflow.ai/ We’re excited to announce that PCBWay and ProtoFlow have teamed up to make the journey from PCB design to manufacturing easier. As AI continues to transform the way we work, ProtoFlow brings AI-assisted capabilities to PCB design, helping users design, simulate, and validate their boards before manufacturing. ProtoFlow takes PCBWay’s manufacturing requirements into account during the design process and checks the board for manufacturability before export, helping users identify and address potential issues early. Its built-in simulation tools and AI agent also allow users to test designs against their own requirements and refine them until all checks pass. Once the design is ready, users can send their Gerber, BOM, and coordinate files directly to PCBWay with just one click and go straight to the quotation page. This integration creates a smoother workflow from AI-assisted design to PCB manufacturing, helping makers and engineers turn their ideas into reality with greater ease: Ready to give it a try? Explore ProtoFlow and enjoy a smoother journey from PCB design to manufacturing with PCBWay! Visit ProtoFlow: https://www.protoflow.ai/ Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Get $29 PCB Assembly and Meet the Requirements How to Get $29 PCB Assembly and Meet the Requirements by: Mila Oct 21,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Assembly PCBWay's $29 PCB assembly offer provides a special assembly service price for eligible PCB prototypes. It is designed for relatively simple projects with limited assembly requirements. Not every PCB assembly project qualifies for this offer. Your project must meet the technical requirements listed below, and the promotion is subject to customer eligibility and usage limits. $29 PCB Assembly Requirements To qualify for the $29 PCB assembly offer, your project must meet all of the following requirements: Component Sourcing: All components must be supplied by PCBWay. PCB Type: Only rigid PCBs are eligible. Flex PCBs and rigid-flex PCBs are not supported by this offer. Assembly Quantity: No more than 20 boards per order. Components per Board: Each board can have a maximum of 200 components. Total Component Quantity: The total number of components across the order cannot exceed 600. Unique Component Types: The project can include no more than 100 different component types. Through-Hole Solder Joints: The total number of through-hole solder joints cannot exceed 100. All limits are inclusive. For example, an order for exactly 20 boards or a project with exactly 100 different component types can qualify, provided that all other requirements are also met. Important: Meeting these technical requirements does not automatically guarantee the promotional price. Your order must also meet the applicable customer eligibility and monthly usage limits. How Often Can You Use the $29 PCB Assembly Offer? The $29 PCB assembly promotion has a monthly usage limit based on customer status. New customers: Eligible new customers can use the offer once per month. Returning customers: Eligible returning customers can use the offer up to twice per month. If you submit multiple orders at the same time, only one eligible order can receive the $29 promotional price. The remaining orders will be charged at their applicable rates. Please note that each order must meet all the technical requirements to qualify for the promotion. The monthly usage limit does not mean that every order you submit will receive the special price. How to Get $29 PCB Assembly on PCBWay Follow these steps to get started. Step 1: Prepare your PCB design files Prepare your Gerber files, Bill of Materials (BOM), and pick-and-place file, as applicable to your project. Step 2: Check your project requirements Confirm that your project uses rigid PCBs, that all components will be supplied by PCBWay, and that your assembly quantity and component counts are within the specified limits. Step 3: Submit your assembly order Visit the PCBWay PCB Assembly Service page and submit your PCB assembly files and requirements. Step 4: Confirm your eligibility Check your eligibility for the promotion and make sure you have not exceeded the applicable usage limit. The final price is subject to order review and confirmation. Frequently Asked Questions -Can I use the $29 PCB assembly offer for flex PCBs or rigid-flex PCBs? No. The promotion is available for rigid PCBs only. Flex PCBs and rigid-flex PCBs are excluded. -Can I supply my own components? No. All components must be supplied by PCBWay to qualify for this offer. -Can I order more than 20 boards? No. The maximum eligible assembly quantity is 20 boards per order. -How many components can my PCB have? Each board can have no more than 200 components, and the total component quantity across the order cannot exceed 600. -Is there a limit on component types? Yes. The project can include no more than 100 different component types. -Are through-hole components allowed? Projects with through-hole components may qualify, provided that the total number of through-hole solder joints does not exceed 100 and all other requirements are met. -Can I apply the $29 price to multiple orders submitted at once? No. Only one eligible order can receive the promotional price when multiple orders are submitted together. -Can I use the offer again next month? The promotion may be available again according to the applicable monthly usage limit. Please check your eligibility before placing another order. -Does the $29 price cover my entire PCB project? The $29 offer is a special PCB assembly price, not necessarily the total cost of your project. PCB fabrication, components, shipping, and other applicable charges may be quoted separately. PCBWay's $29 PCB assembly offer is designed to make simple PCB prototypes more affordable. Verify Now Blog > Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Analog vs Digital Circuits: Understanding Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips by: Mila Sep 30,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout analog vs digital circuits analog and digital circuits analog circuits digital circuits mixed signal PCB design We often say that the world of chips consists of only 0s and 1s. But more accurately, digital circuits use defined voltage ranges to represent discrete logic states, while the real world is clearly not like that. Human voices have different volumes, light has different levels of brightness, temperature changes continuously, and radio waves do not simply jump between 0 V and 1 V. So here is the question: If CPUs mainly process digital data, how can a smartphone hear sound, capture photos, connect to a cellular network, and charge its battery? The answer lies in three types of chips: digital chips, analog chips, and mixed-signal chips. Understanding the differences between them is also important for PCB layout , because digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits have different requirements for signal integrity, grounding, power, and noise control. （class B analog audio amplifier） Analog vs Digital Circuits: What Is the Difference? The key difference between analog vs digital circuits is how they represent and process signals. Digital signals focus on discrete states. In a typical digital circuit, voltage is divided into high and low ranges, which are interpreted as 1 and 0. As long as the signal remains within the specified range, small amounts of noise usually do not change the logic result. Analog signals, on the other hand, preserve continuous changes. The small voltage generated by a microphone, the radio-frequency signal received by an antenna, changes in temperature detected by a sensor, and the voltage and current during battery charging and discharging can all vary continuously over time and amplitude. A simple way to understand analog and digital circuits is: A digital signal is like written text. It mainly cares about which character is being represented. An analog signal is like speech. It contains not only information, but also volume, tone, speed, and many subtle changes. In other words, digital circuits are good at processing discrete information, while analog circuits directly interact with continuously changing signals from the real world. （Analog vs Digital Signals） Digital Chips: Computing, Control, and Memory Digital chips are best suited to problems that can be clearly defined and represented as discrete data. Common digital chips include: CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs; MCUs and various controllers; DRAM, SRAM, and NAND Flash; FPGAs; Digital interface and network processing chips. Digital circuits are built from large numbers of logic gates, flip-flops, registers, and memory cells. Driven by a clock, data flows and is processed according to defined rules. Their biggest advantage is their high level of abstraction. Engineers can move from transistors to logic gates, then to adders, processors, instructions, and software. This allows complex systems to be designed, verified, and optimized at different levels of abstraction. Digital chips are particularly suitable for: Executing programs; Storing data; Implementing complex control functions; Performing large-scale logic and mathematical operations; Precisely coordinating different functions within a system. However, digital circuits themselves cannot directly process continuously changing analog signals. A CPU cannot simply take the tiny analog voltage generated by a microphone and process it as digital data. Nor can it directly turn a string of binary data into the continuous analog signal needed to drive a speaker. This is where analog circuits and mixed-signal circuits come in. Analog Chips: Connecting Electronics to the Real World Analog chips process continuously changing voltages and currents. They do not necessarily focus on extremely large amounts of digital logic, but they often determine whether a device can hear clearly, measure accurately, transmit effectively, and charge efficiently. Typical analog and analog-intensive chips include: Operational amplifiers and comparators; Voltage references and analog front ends; Power management chips such as LDOs and DC-DC converters; Audio amplifiers; Analog circuits used in RF front ends. The problems that analog circuits need to solve are very much connected to the real world: How do you amplify a weak signal? How do you filter out unwanted noise? How do you keep an output voltage stable? How do you maintain performance when temperature and supply voltage change? Analog design is challenging because many real-world details cannot simply be abstracted away. Transistor characteristics, temperature, noise, power-supply fluctuations, parasitic resistance, and parasitic capacitance can all affect the final result. Digital circuits mainly need to determine whether a signal should be recognized as 1 or 0, so many small variations can be tolerated. Analog circuits, however, often need to pay close attention to the actual signal amplitude, noise, distortion, and offset. For example, for an analog amplifier, whether the output is 0.999 V or 1.001 V may affect the final measurement or control result. Mixed-Signal Chips: Bridging the Analog and Digital Worlds Real-world electronic devices need both analog and digital processing. That is why mixed-signal chips exist. They integrate analog and digital circuits into the same chip or system so that the two types of circuits can work together. The most typical bridge is: ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter): Converts analog signals into digital data; DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter): Converts digital data back into analog signals. The process can be simplified as: Real world → Analog signal → ADC → Digital data → Digital processing → DAC → Analog signal → Real world For example, during audio recording and playback, a microphone first converts sound into an analog electrical signal. The analog front end processes the signal, and an ADC converts it into digital data. After the digital processor stores and processes the data, a DAC converts it back into an analog signal, which is then amplified and reproduced by a speaker. A mixed-signal chip is not simply a combination of an ADC and a DAC. It may also contain: ADCs and DACs; PLLs and clock circuits; High-speed SerDes interfaces; Analog front ends; Digital calibration and control logic. These circuits need to work together within the same system, which is one reason mixed-signal design can be challenging. How Do Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Work Together in a Smartphone? A smartphone is a typical example of a system that combines all three types of chips. It needs to process digital data while constantly interacting with the analog signals of the real world. When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
