When You Take a Photo The image sensor converts light into electrical signals; The analog front end amplifies and processes the weak signals; The ADC converts the analog signals into digital data; The ISP performs noise reduction, white balance, and color processing; The CPU, GPU, NPU, and other digital processing units continue with computation, compression, display, and AI recognition. The overall process is essentially: Light → Analog electrical signal → Digital image data → Digital processing When You Connect to a Cellular Network The antenna receives radio-frequency signals; The RF front end amplifies, filters, and converts the signals; An ADC and related circuits convert the analog signal into digital samples; The baseband processor performs demodulation, error correction, and protocol processing. The signal path can be simplified as: Radio waves → Analog RF signal → Digital data → Baseband processing When You Charge Your Smartphone Power management and charging circuits convert and regulate the input voltage and current; The system monitors battery voltage, temperature, and charging status; Power devices handle the main energy conversion; Digital control logic adjusts the charging strategy according to system conditions. So, a smartphone is not purely a “digital device.” Digital, Analog, and Mixed-Signal Chips Compared These three types do not simply replace one another. In real electronic systems, they usually need to work together. Why Are Analog Chips Difficult to Replace? Many people see advanced digital chips with tens of billions of transistors and assume that analog chips must be relatively simple. In reality, the difficulty of analog design is not simply about transistor count. It lies in the trade-offs among device characteristics, process technology, noise, temperature, matching, and parasitic effects. Digital design can make extensive use of standard cells and automated tools. Analog circuits, however, often require repeated optimization based on process technology, device characteristics, and the application environment. The same circuit can behave differently when implemented on a different process. Even a seemingly insignificant trace in the layout can introduce additional parasitic effects, noise coupling, or matching problems. As a result, analog chip design often relies heavily on accumulated process and design experience, along with extensive verification and reliability testing. Why Do These Differences Matter in PCB Design? The differences between analog and digital circuits inside a chip also extend to PCB design. Digital circuits typically require careful consideration of signal integrity, crosstalk, clocks, and return paths, while analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, grounding, power stability, and sensitive signal integrity. For mixed signal PCB design, these issues often exist at the same time. For example, an ADC or DAC may connect to analog signals on one side and digital processing circuitry on the other. If the layout, power distribution, grounding, or return paths are not properly designed, noise generated by digital circuits can couple into sensitive analog signals. Therefore, mixed-signal PCB design often requires careful consideration of: Analog and digital circuit placement; Power and ground design; Return paths for high-speed digital signals; Noise control around ADCs and DACs; Decoupling capacitors and power integrity; Isolation between sensitive analog signals and high-speed digital signals. This is why understanding the differences between analog and digital circuits is important not only for chip designers, but also for PCB designers. Conclusion Digital chips have not replaced analog chips, and analog chips are not a “lower-end” version of digital chips. They serve different purposes: Digital chips handle computing, control, and memory. Analog chips handle sensing, amplification, and driving. Mixed-signal chips connect and translate between the two. Without digital chips, electronic devices would struggle to perform complex computations. Without analog chips, even the most powerful processor could not directly hear, see, sense, or interact with the real world. And in today's electronic devices, it is rarely one type of chip working alone. Instead, digital, analog, and mixed-signal circuits work together as one system. The smartphones, computers, vehicles, and smart devices we use every day are ultimately the result of these three worlds working together. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Are More PCB Decoupling Capacitors Always Better? by: Mila Oct 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor PCB decoupling capacitor decoupling capacitor placement PCB power integrity If you have ever designed a PCB schematic , you have probably placed a familiar trio of capacitors near a chip’s power pins: 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF.It seems like a safe bet. Different capacitance values, neatly arranged, ready to keep the power supply stable and suppress noise. But is this tried-and-tested combination always the best choice? When it comes to decoupling capacitors, does adding more always mean better performance? Not necessarily. Effective decoupling depends on more than capacitance alone. Component characteristics, parasitic effects, and PCB layout all play a role. Understanding ESR, ESL, and Self-Resonant Frequenc Circuit theory tells us that the impedance of an ideal capacitor decreases as frequency increases. Real capacitors, however, are not quite so simple. They have two important parasitic parameters: equivalent series resistance (ESR) and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL deserves particular attention. As frequency increases, the capacitive impedance decreases until the capacitor reaches its self-resonant frequency (SRF). Around this frequency, the capacitor typically exhibits its minimum impedance. Beyond SRF, parasitic inductance begins to dominate, and impedance increases with frequency. In other words, a capacitor does not become more effective at filtering noise simply because the frequency keeps rising. Above its SRF, its ability to suppress higher-frequency noise may be limited. That is why selecting a PCB decoupling capacitor requires more than checking its nominal capacitance. You also need to understand how its impedance changes with frequency. How Different Capacitance Values Work Together Capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics. When selected appropriately, they can help maintain low impedance across a wider frequency range in the power distribution network (PDN). 10 µF capacitors are commonly used to provide local charge storage and help reduce impedance over certain low- to mid-frequency ranges. Their actual performance depends on the capacitor type, package, ESR, ESL, and operating voltage. For lower-frequency ripple, the voltage regulator, bulk capacitors, and the overall power network must also be considered. 1 µF capacitors can complement larger and smaller capacitors by helping shape the impedance response over particular frequency ranges. However, whether they effectively fill the gap between other capacitance values depends on the actual impedance curves, not just the nominal capacitance. 0.1 µF capacitors are commonly used for high-frequency decoupling near chip power pins. Although their capacitance is smaller, they can often be placed in compact packages with short connection paths, helping reduce parasitic inductance and improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Each has its strengths, and combining them can make sense. However, 10 µF, 1 µF, and 0.1 µF are not a universal combination with three fixed frequency ranges. Their effective operating ranges may overlap, and the appropriate values depend on the chip’s requirements, component characteristics, and PCB layout. （capacitor unit conversion chart） How Dielectric and Package Size Affect Decoupling （MLCC Package Size and Decoupling Performance） Two factors that deserve more attention than capacitance alone are dielectric material and package size. Let's start with the dielectric. Suppose you choose a 10 µF ceramic capacitor with a Y5V or Z5U dielectric because it is inexpensive and offers the desired nominal capacitance. Once operating conditions come into play, its capacitance may change significantly with temperature and DC bias voltage. That does not mean these dielectric types are unsuitable for every application. However, their characteristics may make them less suitable for decoupling applications that require stable capacitance. For common power supply decoupling applications, X7R and X5R are often preferred dielectric types. But choosing either one does not guarantee that the nominal capacitance will be available under operating conditions. Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), especially those with high capacitance in small packages, can experience significant capacitance loss under DC bias. Always check the manufacturer's datasheet, particularly the DC bias curve, to determine how much effective capacitance remains at the actual operating voltage. For example, a nominal 10 µF X5R capacitor may provide substantially less capacitance at a particular operating voltage and package size. Even if several capacitors are installed, the effective decoupling capacitance may still be insufficient. Now, let's look at package size. Two 0.1 µF capacitors in 0402 and 0805 packages may have different parasitic characteristics and high-frequency performance. Under otherwise comparable conditions, a smaller package can help reduce component parasitics and the inductance of the mounting loop. However, the actual improvement depends on the component structure, terminal design, and PCB layout. You cannot assume that ESL decreases by a fixed percentage every time the package size is reduced. Sometimes, optimizing the package size and mounting loop can be more effective than simply increasing capacitance. That said, smaller is not always better. Capacitance requirements, voltage rating, soldering reliability, and manufacturing constraints must also be considered. How Parasitics and Anti-Resonance Affect PCB Decoupling Some designers assume that if capacitors with different values can cover different frequency ranges, adding more of them should suppress noise across the board. That sounds reasonable in theory, but reality is more complicated. When multiple capacitors are connected in parallel, their capacitance, ESR, ESL, and PCB interconnect parasitics interact to form a complex impedance network. Under certain conditions, this network can produce an anti-resonance peak, causing the impedance of the power distribution network to rise at a particular frequency. In simple terms, some capacitor branches may behave capacitively while others behave inductively at that frequency. Their interaction, together with interconnect parasitics, can create an impedance peak. The peak's frequency and magnitude depend on the component parameters, connection topology, PCB power planes, and mounting loops. Simply adding or removing capacitors does not guarantee a solution. PCB space is also limited. Adding too many capacitors can crowd routing areas and force some components farther away from the chip's power pins. Longer connection paths can increase loop inductance and weaken high-frequency decoupling performance. So, do not focus only on how many capacitors appear in the schematic. Where they are placed, how they are connected, and how the overall network behaves are equally important. Consider a design example. Suppose a simulation of an FPGA power distribution network reveals a pronounced anti-resonance peak. Adding more capacitors with different capacitance values may not solve the problem and could even make the peak more pronounced. A better approach is to examine the impedance curve, analyze the capacitors' ESR and ESL, evaluate interconnect parasitics, and review the layout. The capacitor combination and connection topology can then be adjusted as needed. In some cases, a more optimized design may use fewer capacitors. However, removing capacitors without checking the impedance response can also increase impedance in certain frequency ranges. The real goal is not to minimize the number of capacitors, but to optimize the impedance of the entire power distribution network. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Design: Three Key Principles It comes down to three key principles. 1. Start with the requirements, not guesswork. For high-speed digital circuits, the target impedance method can help guide decoupling design: Here, (Delta V) is the allowable power supply voltage variation, and (Delta I) is the transient current change that the power distribution network must support. First, determine the allowable voltage variation based on the chip's power requirements. Then estimate the target impedance and evaluate the required capacitance values, capacitor count, and placement based on the load's transient behavior and the PDN impedance profile. Of course, target impedance is only one part of the design process. Voltage regulator response, chip packaging, PCB power planes, and the actual capacitor characteristics must also be considered. Rather than copying a fixed capacitor combination, start by understanding what the circuit actually needs. 2. Placement matters more than quantity. A decoupling capacitor should be placed as close as practical to its corresponding chip power pin. The current loop between the power pin, capacitor, and ground plane should be kept short. Connect the capacitor's ground terminal to a continuous ground plane through a via placed as close to the ground pad as practical. For high-frequency decoupling, multiple ground vias may help reduce loop inductance, depending on the layout and current path. However, two vias are not mandatory in every design. Also, proximity alone does not guarantee a good layout. Poor power routing, an indirect ground path, or an unsuitable via connection can still introduce significant parasitic inductance. Remember: High-frequency decoupling is not just about placing a capacitor close to the chip. It is about creating a short, low-inductance current loop. This is one of the most important considerations in decoupling capacitor placement and effective PCB layout. 3. Know when to simplify—but do not remove capacitors blindly. Not every chip needs the full 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination. For low-speed circuits with modest transient current demands, a small number of decoupling capacitors may be sufficient, provided the device requirements are met. High-speed FPGAs, processors, and other devices with demanding transient loads may require a more complex capacitor network and a carefully designed power distribution system. The appropriate number and values of capacitors should be determined using the chip manufacturer's recommendations, target impedance, and design verification results. A well-designed network is more reliable than a collection of capacitors added without a clear purpose. （Good vs. Poor Decoupling Capacitor Placement） The 0.1 µF, 1 µF, and 10 µF combination is a useful engineering starting point, not a universal rule. There is a sound reason behind it: capacitors with different capacitance values have different impedance characteristics, and a suitable combination can improve power distribution network performance across different frequency ranges. But that does not mean more capacitance is always better—or that fewer capacitors automatically make a better design. Good power supply design is not about how many capacitors you solder onto a board. It is about understanding frequency, impedance, component characteristics, and PCB layout . Do not simply copy a reference design and place capacitors without understanding why they are there. Learn to evaluate the actual requirements and make informed design decisions. Sometimes, the problem is not that you need more capacitors. It is that the wrong capacitor was selected—or the first one was placed incorrectly. Less guesswork, more deliberate design. That is the principle behind effective decoupling capacitor selection and PCB power integrity. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending Flex PCB Design Guidelines for Reliable Bending by: Mila Oct 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout flex PCB design flex PCB bend radius flexible PCB design guidelines Unlike rigid PCBs, flexible PCBs (FPCs) can bend and fold to fit into compact electronic devices. They are widely used in smartphones, laptops, printers, and other products where space is limited or components need to move. However, flexibility does not mean an FPC can bend without limits. Poorly designed bend areas can lead to copper trace cracks, delamination, or premature failure, especially in applications involving repeated bending. A reliable flex PCB design must account for bend radius, trace routing, copper foil selection, and stiffener placement. In this guide, we’ll look at the key design considerations for FPC bend areas and how to improve their reliability in both static and dynamic bending applications. Three Common Flex PCB Bend Area Design Mistakes 1. Keep Vias Out of the Bend Area Vias are one of the key structures to watch when designing a flex PCB bend area. To simplify routing, inexperienced designers may place vias close to a bend line to change layers. However, repeated bending can eventually cause trace fractures and electrical failures. The reason is straightforward: vias introduce structural transitions between the copper plating, pads, and substrate. Differences in material properties and geometry can affect local stress distribution. During repeated bending, stress may concentrate around the via, leading to copper fatigue and crack propagation over time. Eventually, the electrical connection may fail. Design tip: Avoid placing through-holes, blind vias, or buried vias within the active bend area. If layer transitions are necessary, move the vias outside the bend area whenever possible. The required clearance depends on the bend geometry, board thickness, and manufacturer guidelines. A clearance of at least 1 mm can serve as an initial layout reference, but it is not a universal requirement for every FPC. 2. Keep Components Out of the Bend Area Resistors, capacitors, ICs, connectors, and other SMT components should generally not be placed in areas that undergo repeated bending. Components are relatively rigid, while the flexible substrate deforms during bending. If a component sits within the bend area, additional mechanical stress may develop around its body, pads, and solder joints. Brittle components, such as ceramic capacitors, require particular attention because both solder joint cracking and component body damage are possible. Design tip: Place components in rigid sections or reinforced areas, away from the actual bending region. A clearance of 2 mm beyond the bend boundary can serve as an initial reference, but the final distance should account for component size, stiffener geometry, and the actual bending range. 3. Do Not Choose Trace Direction Based on Routing Convenience Alone Trace direction affects how mechanical stress is distributed during bending. However, no single routing angle is best for every FPC structure. When routing through a bend area, consider the actual bending axis, bending direction, and trace distribution. Avoid sharp corners, abrupt width changes, and locally crowded traces, as these features can create stress concentrations. Traces perpendicular to the bending axis: This arrangement may be appropriate for traces crossing the bend area in certain single-axis bending structures, but it must be evaluated against the actual bending geometry. Traces parallel to the bending axis: Whether this arrangement is suitable depends on the specific structure. It should not automatically be classified as the most failure-prone direction. Traces at 45°: Angled routing may work in certain layouts, but its bending life cannot simply be assumed to fall between that of perpendicular and parallel traces. For dynamic flex PCB applications, prioritize smooth, continuous traces, avoid sharp turns and abrupt geometry changes, and verify reliability through appropriate bending tests. (flex PCB bend area design with via and component keepout zones) How to Choose the Right Flex PCB Bend Radius When designing an FPC, some engineers focus mainly on whether it fits inside the enclosure. Reducing the bend radius too much may make assembly easier, but it can also shorten the product's service life. First, distinguish between static and dynamic bending. Their design requirements are different. Static bending: The FPC is bent during assembly and then remains in a relatively fixed position. Internal cables that do not move during normal operation are typical examples. A relatively small bend radius may be acceptable, provided it meets the requirements of the specific material and structure. Dynamic bending: The FPC repeatedly bends during operation. Examples include foldable phone hinges, printer head cables, and robotic joints. These applications place greater demands on copper fatigue resistance, bend radius, and overall structural design. For preliminary flex PCB design, the following values can serve as starting points: Static bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 6 times the total board thickness may be used as an initial reference. Dynamic bending: A minimum bend radius of approximately 10 times the total board thickness or greater may be used as an initial reference. These ratios are not universal standards. The actual requirement depends on factors such as single-sided or double-sided construction, copper layer count, copper foil type, material thickness, and the target number of bending cycles. For applications requiring a long flex life, follow the design guidelines provided by the material supplier or FPC manufacturer. For example, if an FPC has a total thickness of 0.2 mm, the preliminary reference values would be: Static bend radius: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2 mm Dynamic bend radius: 0.2 × 10 = 2.0 mm These figures illustrate the calculation method only. They should not be treated as minimum design limits for every 0.2 mm FPC. An excessively small bend radius can cause copper fatigue cracking, coverlay or substrate delamination, and, in severe cases, substrate damage. Any of these failures can eventually render the flexible circuit unusable. RA Copper vs. ED Copper for Flex PCBs Copper foil is an essential part of the FPC's conductive structure and a key factor in repeated-bending reliability. When choosing copper foil, consider whether the application involves static or dynamic bending rather than focusing on cost alone. Electrodeposited copper (ED copper): ED copper is produced through an electrodeposition process and offers mature manufacturing processes and cost advantages. Its grain structure differs from that of rolled copper, and its fatigue performance should be evaluated carefully for repeated-bending applications. For applications involving relatively few bending cycles, ED copper may be considered depending on the specific design and manufacturer recommendations. Rolled-annealed copper (RA copper): RA copper is produced through rolling and annealing. It generally offers good ductility and flexing performance, making it suitable for FPCs that require a longer dynamic flex life. Although it typically costs more, it may help improve reliability in applications involving repeated bending. The key takeaway is simple: For static applications, select copper foil based on cost and performance requirements. For dynamic applications with high cycle counts, RA copper is generally the preferred starting point, subject to verification of the bend radius, copper thickness, and target service life. Flex PCB Routing Guidelines for Reliable Bending In addition to the major design restrictions discussed above, several details deserve attention during flex PCB routing and layout. Trace direction: Determine the routing direction based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces should remain smooth and continuous, with unnecessary sharp turns avoided. Trace width and spacing: Choose appropriate trace widths and spacing to meet electrical and manufacturing requirements. Distribute multiple traces evenly across the bend area instead of crowding them into one section. The final dimensions should account for the bending structure, copper thickness, and manufacturing capabilities rather than relying on a fixed width-to-spacing ratio. Corners and width transitions: Use rounded corners or smooth transitions wherever practical. Avoid sharp corners and abrupt changes in trace width to reduce stress concentrations. Minimize unnecessary crossovers and layer transitions within the bend area. Coverlay: Flexible coverlay is commonly used to protect copper traces in bend areas and reduce the risk of wear and oxidation. Position coverlay openings carefully, keeping coverlay edges away from regions of high mechanical stress. Confirm the required coverage and manufacturing details for the specific design. FPC Stiffeners: Stainless Steel vs. PI Stiffeners increase local rigidity in an FPC. They are commonly used beneath connectors, gold fingers, and SMT components. However, stiffeners should not extend into the active bend area where the FPC needs to flex freely. Stainless steel stiffeners: Stainless steel provides relatively high rigidity and is commonly available in thicknesses of approximately 0.1–0.3 mm. It is often used behind connectors and gold fingers to improve structural support and withstand insertion and removal forces. Pay attention to edge geometry and transitions to prevent sharp edges from damaging the FPC substrate. PI stiffeners: Polyimide (PI) stiffeners are generally thinner and more flexible than metal stiffeners. They can be used beneath certain SMT components or in areas that require localized reinforcement while retaining some flexibility. Their actual rigidity depends on the material thickness and structure. Stress concentrations near stiffener edges should also be considered. Regardless of the stiffener type, keep it outside the active bend area. The required clearance depends on the bending range, stiffener thickness, and overall structure. A fixed 2 mm clearance alone cannot guarantee a reliable design. No components or pads unsuitable for bending are placed within the bend area. Trace direction has been evaluated based on the actual bending axis and motion. Traces use smooth transitions without sharp corners or abrupt width changes. Multiple traces are distributed evenly to avoid local congestion. The copper foil type matches the static or dynamic bending requirements. The bend radius has been calculated and checked against material and manufacturer requirements. Layer count, copper thickness, and structural design have been evaluated for high-cycle applications. Coverlay openings and edges are positioned away from high-stress regions. Stiffeners remain outside the active bend area, with appropriate edge transitions. A suitable flex-life test plan has been established for critical dynamic applications. Ultimately, successful flex PCB design comes down to controlling bending strain, minimizing local stress concentrations, and ensuring that the materials and structure meet the required flex life. Keep vias and components out of active bend areas, route traces smoothly, allow sufficient bend radius, and select copper foil carefully for dynamic applications. For products that undergo repeated bending, validate the design through testing rather than relying on general rules of thumb alone. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Reduce Crosstalk in PCB Routing: Spacing, 3W Rule, and More How to Reduce Crosstalk in PCB Routing: Spacing, 3W Rule, and More by: Mila Oct 13,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB routing signal integrity，PCB crosstalk，3W rule PCB Many hardware and PCB layout engineers rely heavily on experience when dealing with crosstalk. Routes that are too close may cause interference, while increasing spacing can make routing difficult. Some designers apply the 3W rule to every high-speed signal, while others simply move sensitive traces farther away from potential noise sources. Yet after fabrication, unexpected problems may still appear, including waveform distortion, communication errors, clock instability, and fluctuations in low-level signals. In some cases, PCB crosstalk is part of the problem. Crosstalk is not an unpredictable phenomenon. It can be analyzed, simulated, and controlled through proper PCB routing and layout design. So, how does crosstalk occur? How do trace spacing and parallel routing length affect interference? And why is the widely used 3W rule not a universal solution? Understanding these factors can help you make better routing decisions and improve signal integrity without relying on guesswork. When two traces are close together and run parallel for a considerable distance, electromagnetic energy from the aggressor can couple into the victim, introducing unwanted noise voltage or current. This phenomenon is known as PCB crosstalk—essentially, electromagnetic coupling between neighboring signal paths. Several key factors influence the amount of crosstalk: Trace spacing: Under otherwise comparable conditions, smaller spacing generally increases coupling and makes crosstalk more pronounced. Parallel routing length: Longer parallel runs provide more opportunity for electromagnetic coupling. The actual impact depends on propagation delay, signal edge rate, and transmission-line structure. Signal edge rate: Faster rise and fall times generally introduce more high-frequency content, making high-frequency coupling effects more significant. Reference planes and stackup: Continuous reference planes, appropriate dielectric thickness, and suitable layer assignments help control electromagnetic fields and reduce unwanted coupling. These factors explain why slowly changing signals are often easier to manage, while high-speed clocks, DDR interfaces, and other fast signals can become more sensitive to relatively small changes in routing geometry. How Does Trace Spacing Affect Crosstalk? It is tempting to assume that doubling the spacing between traces will halve—or even reduce to one-quarter—the crosstalk. In practice, however, there is no universal mathematical relationship between trace spacing and crosstalk that applies to every PCB design. The coupling between PCB traces depends on several variables, including trace width, spacing, dielectric thickness, reference planes, parallel length, and signal edge rate. Therefore, a simple spacing ratio cannot reliably predict the resulting reduction in crosstalk. In general, increasing the spacing between adjacent traces reduces electromagnetic coupling. This can be particularly effective when the original spacing is very small. However, increasing spacing does not guarantee a fixed percentage reduction in crosstalk. To estimate the actual improvement, designers should evaluate the specific stackup, trace geometry, and signal characteristics through simulation or measurement. In practical PCB routing, spacing rules provide a useful starting point. Signal integrity simulation and crosstalk budgets can then help determine whether the final layout meets the required performance. Capacitive and Inductive Coupling in PCB Routing Crosstalk between PCB traces primarily occurs through electric-field and magnetic-field coupling, commonly described as capacitive coupling and inductive coupling. Both mechanisms may contribute to the overall interference, although their relative importance depends on the routing structure and signal conditions. 1. Capacitive Coupling: Electric-Field Interference Adjacent PCB traces naturally form a parasitic capacitance. When the voltage on the aggressor changes rapidly, current can couple into the victim through this parasitic capacitance. The faster the voltage changes (dv/dt), the more important capacitive coupling may become. In simple terms, faster voltage transitions can increase the impact of capacitive coupling. Clock signals, PWM signals, and fast-switching control signals are common sources of this type of interference. 2. Inductive Coupling: Magnetic-Field Interference Adjacent traces also have mutual inductance. When the current in the aggressor changes rapidly, the surrounding magnetic field changes as well. This changing field can induce an unwanted voltage in the victim. The faster the current changes (di/dt), the more significant inductive coupling may become. In simple terms, rapid current transitions can increase the impact of inductive coupling. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Verify Now Blog > Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT Power Supply Pinout Explained: VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, and BAT by: Mila Oct 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply pinout power supply pins DC-DC converter pins VIN vs VOUT Isn’t VIN the power input and VOUT the output? Many beginner hardware engineers have this question in PCB layout when they first look at power ICs and power module schematics. If a power supply essentially has an input and an output, why are some pins labeled VIN and VOUT, while others are called SW, PH, or BAT? VIN usually refers to the power input, while VOUT refers to the power output. However, neither label necessarily means the voltage is already regulated. SW/PH typically identifies a switching node in a DC-DC converter, where high-frequency switching waveforms are present. BAT is a battery-related pin whose function and current direction depend on the specific IC. These pins serve different purposes. Don’t treat them as interchangeable just because their names look familiar. （Power Supply Pins Explained） SW and PH Pins: Understanding the Switching Node SW stands for Switch, while PH commonly stands for Phase. In many Buck converters, both names refer to the switching node connected to the power switches and the inductor. The exact meaning still depends on the IC and its datasheet. Take a synchronous Buck converter as an example. When the high-side MOSFET Q1 turns on, SW is pulled close to VIN. When the low-side MOSFET Q2 turns on, SW is pulled close to GND. So SW is neither a conventional DC input nor a regulated output. Instead, it rapidly switches between high and low voltage levels. Under ideal steady-state conditions, the average SW voltage is approximately equal to the output voltage: VOUT ≈ D × VIN Here, D is the duty cycle, or the fraction of each switching period during which SW stays high. In an ideal Buck converter, the IC regulates the output voltage by adjusting the PWM duty cycle. Real circuits also have to account for MOSFET voltage drops, parasitic effects, and other losses. Three things you should know 1. In a typical Buck converter, SW connects to the output through an inductor. The inductor and output capacitor work together to transfer energy and filter the switching waveform, providing a relatively stable DC voltage to the load. SW should not be treated as a conventional regulated output. 2. The SW node of an asynchronous Buck converter may go below ground. When the high-side switch turns off and the inductor current flows through the freewheeling diode, SW may be pulled slightly below GND. The actual negative voltage depends on the diode drop, parasitic effects, and switching transients rather than a fixed value. 3. The SW node has a high dv/dt and is a major source of EMI and ringing. When measuring its waveform, use a short probe ground spring or another suitable low-inductance grounding method. Avoid long probe ground leads, which can introduce additional ringing. SW vs. PH: What’s the Difference? Different manufacturers may use different names for similar switching nodes. In multiphase Buck controllers, each phase typically has its own PH or SW node. The switching waveforms usually share the same switching frequency but are phase-shifted relative to one another, which helps explain why PH is a common label. Single-phase converters often use SW as a more straightforward name for the switching node. However, SW, PH, and even LX are not guaranteed to be interchangeable across every IC. When checking a schematic, the safest approach is to read the Pin Description section of the datasheet and confirm the pin's function and recommended connections. BAT Pin Explained: Three Common Applications The BAT label can be misleading if you assume it means "battery output." In reality, it generally identifies a battery-related connection, and its function and current direction depend on the IC's purpose and internal architecture. （SW vs. VOUT in a Buck Converter） Three common BAT pin applications 1. BAT on a battery charger IC Take the TP4056 as an example. Its BAT pin connects to the positive terminal of the battery. During charging, the IC supplies charging current through this pin and monitors the battery voltage. It is not a general-purpose power output intended for arbitrary loads. 2. BAT in a battery-powered system On some PMICs designed to support battery operation, BAT is the battery connection. The IC can draw power from the battery and supply the system through its internal power conversion or distribution circuitry. The exact function depends on the IC architecture. 3. BAT on a power-path management IC A charger with power-path management, such as the BQ24075, typically provides both BAT and SYS connections. When an adapter is connected, the system can be powered from the input supply while the battery charges. When the adapter is removed, the system can switch to battery power. However, voltage dips and power interruptions during the transition depend on the IC's characteristics, system load, and surrounding circuit design. Not every implementation guarantees a completely seamless switchover under all conditions. Remember this: BAT is a battery-related connection, not a general-purpose output. Whether it connects to the battery or the system depends on the datasheet, not the name alone. VIN vs. VOUT vs. SW: Understanding the Differences When a power module provides VIN and VOUT pins, it usually means that a substantial portion of the power conversion circuitry is integrated into the module. You generally don't need to build the entire power stage externally as you would with a more discrete design. Power module vs. DC-DC converter IC Typical examples include TI's LMZM series, ADI's µModule series, and Murata's OKI-78SR series. These modules integrate some or most of the power conversion circuitry. External components, such as input and output capacitors, are generally all you need to connect according to the datasheet. However, not every device with a VOUT pin is a power module. Some integrated DC-DC converters also provide a VOUT pin. The distinction depends on the internal architecture and pin definitions. Many DC-DC converter ICs that use an external inductor, such as the TPS54331, MP2359, and LMR14030, expose an SW pin. The inductor, output capacitor, and feedback resistors typically need to be designed externally, and some devices also require an external compensation network. This approach offers greater design flexibility, but it also demands more attention to PCB layout, power-stage loops, and EMI control. SW Pin PCB Layout: Copper Area and EMI Considerations You've probably heard that "the SW copper area should be as small as possible." There's a good reason for this advice, but smaller isn't automatically better in every respect. SW is a high-dv/dt node. An unnecessarily large copper area can increase parasitic capacitance and electromagnetic radiation. At the same time, switching current flows through this node, so its copper geometry must also meet current-carrying, thermal, and parasitic requirements. PCB layout comparison of SW nodes A more practical approach is to keep the SW copper area compact while meeting current-carrying and thermal requirements. Avoid unnecessarily large copper pours, but don't compromise electrical or thermal performance just to minimize the area. The high-frequency current loop deserves just as much attention. Place the input bypass capacitor close to the power switching loop to minimize its area. The placement of the SW copper relative to adjacent ground planes should be evaluated based on the stackup, parasitic capacitance, and EMI requirements. Also, keep feedback traces away from noisy nodes such as SW whenever possible. These layout practices can help improve EMI performance and reduce switching waveform ringing. For more practical tips on power supply PCB layout, including switching loop optimization, SW node routing, and grounding, see our guide to DCDC Power PCB Layout Guidelines . Common Power Supply Pins and Their Functions Let's review some of the most common pins you'll encounter on power ICs. Common power supply pin overview COMP deserves special attention. It's easy to mistake COMP for an input, but on power controllers with external compensation, COMP is typically the output of the error amplifier. An RC compensation network may be connected according to the datasheet's recommendations. FB is typically the feedback input. The IC senses the output voltage through this pin, often using a resistor divider, and compares it with an internal reference. PG/PGOOD indicates the power-good status. An open-drain output is common and requires a pull-up resistor as specified in the datasheet, although not all devices use the same output structure. In addition, EN is typically used to enable or disable the IC, while GND/PGND refers to ground or power-ground connections. Follow the recommended grounding arrangement for the specific device. A quick reference table for common power supply pins These are common pin names and functions, not universal definitions. Always refer to the datasheet for the specific device you're using. Power supply pin names are more than just labels. Understanding the functions of VIN, VOUT, SW, PH, BAT, FB, COMP, and PG can help you interpret a circuit more accurately, follow the power flow, and identify potential issues during debugging. However, pin names alone do not tell the whole story. Always check the IC datasheet to confirm each pin’s function and recommended connections. During PCB layout , pay particular attention to switching nodes, feedback paths, and grounding. Proper component placement and routing can help reduce noise, improve power integrity, and ensure stable operation. Whether you’re designing a simple power supply or a more complex DC-DC converter, understanding these pins is an important step toward reliable PCB design. Verify Now Blog > Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips Reflow Soldering vs. Wave Soldering: Key Differences and PCB Design Tips by: Mila Oct 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Reflow Soldering Wave Soldering SMT vs. THT PCB Assembly PCB Soldering As hardware engineers, we design the PCB, select the components, and send the Gerber files to the manufacturer. But have you ever wondered why some components go through reflow soldering while others require wave soldering? Both processes melt solder to form electrical and mechanical connections, so why does a production line need two different types of equipment? The reason is not that equipment manufacturers are making the process unnecessarily complicated. The main difference between reflow soldering and wave soldering lies in how the solder reaches the joints and which types of components each process is best suited for. For hardware engineers, understanding these two processes is more than just useful knowledge. It can affect PCB layout , component selection, pad design, and even troubleshooting during manufacturing. How Reflow Soldering Works Reflow soldering is primarily used for surface-mount technology (SMT) components, such as resistors, capacitors, SOPs, QFNs, and BGAs. The basic process is straightforward: solder paste is first printed onto the PCB pads, and the components are then placed on the board. Next, the PCB assembly passes through a reflow oven, where the solder paste goes through several stages, including preheating, heating, time above the liquidus temperature, and cooling. These stages allow the solder to melt, wet the surfaces, and solidify to form reliable joints. One detail that is easy to overlook is that reflow soldering is not simply about heating the entire PCB to a fixed temperature. The temperature profile over time must be carefully controlled. Taking the common SAC305 lead-free solder alloy as an example, its melting range is approximately 217–220°C. During reflow, the solder joint temperature must rise above the liquidus temperature and remain there for a certain period. However, the peak temperature, time above liquidus, and heating and cooling rates depend on factors such as the solder paste, component temperature limits, and PCB thermal mass. These parameters cannot be applied universally to every board. （reflow soldering） How Wave Soldering Works Imagine a PCB with small resistors, large connectors, and power pads connected to extensive copper areas. Small components generally have lower thermal mass and heat up quickly, while large components and pads absorb more heat and may heat up more slowly. If the temperature rises too quickly, the small components may approach their peak temperature before the solder on the larger pads has fully melted. On the other hand, increasing the peak temperature too much or extending the time at high temperatures to accommodate the larger pads can increase thermal stress on components, damage the PCB, and raise the risk of solder oxidation. The real challenge of reflow soldering is to ensure that every solder joint receives enough heat, but not excessive heat, while staying within the temperature limits of the components. （wave soldering） Why Reflow Temperature Control Matters Wave soldering works in a more straightforward way. The equipment melts the solder and uses a pump to create a stable wave of molten solder. After the PCB passes through flux application and preheating, its solder side comes into contact with the molten solder. The solder wets the component leads and PCB pads, forming the joints. Traditional wave soldering is most commonly used for through-hole technology (THT) components, such as through-hole connectors, transformers, relay sockets, and some power components. Their leads pass through holes in the PCB, allowing the molten solder to contact the leads and pads from the solder side and form reliable joints. Why Wave Soldering Isn't Suitable for Every PCB Wave soldering brings molten solder into direct contact with the solder side of the PCB. If the board contains a large number of surface-mount components, especially fine-pitch leads or packages with bottom-side pads, solder may bridge adjacent leads or cause soldering defects in components that are unsuitable for this process. However, this does not mean that surface-mount components can never be wave soldered. When wave soldering is used for suitable SMT components, the component orientation, pad spacing, and solder mask design must be considered carefully. In some cases, adhesive is also used to hold the components in place during soldering. PCB travel direction, protruding lead length, and component placement on the solder side must also be taken into account. If the design is unsuitable, even well-adjusted equipment parameters may not be enough to ensure consistent production quality. It is worth noting that reflow soldering is not limited to surface-mount components, nor is wave soldering restricted to through-hole components. Other processes, including selective wave soldering and pin-in-paste soldering (also known as intrusive reflow soldering), are used in actual manufacturing. The appropriate method depends on package structures, component distribution, solder joint reliability, and production requirements. （PCB Assembly） PCB Design Considerations for Reflow and Wave Soldering 1. Component and Pad Design For SMT packages such as QFNs and BGAs, engineers need to consider pad dimensions, solder paste printing, stencil design, and the reflow temperature profile. For through-hole components, important factors include hole diameter, copper thickness, lead dimensions, and solder fill. Package and pad design affect not only electrical performance but also soldering quality during PCB assembly. 2. Copper Distribution and Thermal Management When a power component's pad is connected to a large copper area, the copper can absorb and distribute heat, making it more difficult for the local pad to reach the required temperature. This may prevent the solder from melting sufficiently. During design, engineers should evaluate copper distribution, pad structure, and the actual temperature profile rather than simply increasing the oven temperature to compensate. 3. Common Soldering Defects and Their Causes For example, tombstoning of resistors after reflow soldering may result from uneven heating between the two pads, differences in solder paste volume, or component placement errors. Solder bridging between connector leads after wave soldering may be related to pad spacing, lead orientation, flux application, or wave parameters. When these defects occur, engineers should investigate the PCB design and soldering process alongside the components themselves. Hardware engineers do not necessarily need to operate soldering equipment themselves, but they should understand how their designs affect manufacturability. Reflow soldering focuses on controlling the temperature profile during solder paste melting, while wave soldering focuses on controlling the contact between molten solder and the PCB's solder side. Neither process is universally better than the other. The right choice depends on component packages, PCB layout, and production requirements. Why Do PCBs Need Stitching Vias Along the Board Edge? by: Mila Oct 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout stitching vias PCB EMI shielding PCB return path PCB via stitching Anyone who has worked on PCB layout has probably experienced this: after finishing the layout, you hand the board over to a senior engineer for review. They take a quick look around the board and ask, “Where are the ground vias along the edge?” At first, this may seem unnecessary. After all, the board edge does not carry signal traces. So why are stitching vias placed there? The answer lies in what happens around the edge of a PCB. Properly placed grounding vias can help control electromagnetic coupling, provide a more continuous high-frequency return path, and improve PCB edge shielding. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive designs, that simple row of vias can make a noticeable difference. （Stitching Vias） What Do Ground Vias Along the PCB Edge Actually Do? This row of vias is commonly known as a ground via fence, via fence, or stitching vias. It is not simply a matter of placing a row of vias around the board. Instead, the vias connect ground structures on different PCB layers and create a more continuous electromagnetic boundary along the board edge. For high-speed, RF, and high-reliability PCBs, the main benefits include improving high-frequency return paths, reducing electromagnetic leakage and coupling, and enhancing the continuity of local shielding structures. 1. Reduce Electromagnetic Leakage and Improve EMI Performance The PCB edge is the boundary between copper, dielectric material, and air. When high-speed, clock, or RF signals pass through the board, relatively strong electromagnetic fields may exist around this region. If the reference ground structure around the PCB edge is discontinuous, electromagnetic fields can couple outward through the edge, increasing EMI risks. External interference can also couple into sensitive circuits through the same region. A continuous row of grounding vias creates a low-impedance grounding boundary around the PCB edge. It can help limit the spread of electromagnetic fields around the edge and reduce coupling between the signals and the surrounding environment, improving EMI performance. 2. Provide a More Continuous High-Frequency Return Path High-speed signal return current generally follows a path close to the signal trace and its reference plane. When a PCB contains multiple ground or reference planes, insufficient connections between these planes can force high-frequency return currents to take longer paths, increasing both return path length and loop area. Stitching vias can provide low-impedance connections between different ground layers, giving high-frequency currents a more continuous return path. The more continuous the return path, the smaller the loop area can be, making electromagnetic radiation and crosstalk easier to control. 3. Help Reduce Edge Coupling and Local Resonance For RF, microwave, and high-speed clock PCBs, discontinuities around the board edge can create additional electromagnetic coupling paths and, at certain frequencies, may contribute to unwanted resonance. A continuous row of grounding vias can improve the electromagnetic boundary conditions around the PCB edge, reduce edge coupling, and help suppress local resonance. This is particularly useful in RF regions, shielding areas, and areas with dense high-speed signals, where a properly designed PCB ground via fence can be more effective than simply adding more copper. 4. Provide a Continuous Grounding Point for Shielding Cans RF modules and high-speed precision modules often use metal shielding cans. In this case, grounding vias can work together with the shielding-can solder pad to create a more continuous low-impedance grounding path around the shield. If a shielding can has only a few grounding points, the parasitic inductance of the connection path can affect high-frequency shielding performance. Adding stitching vias around the shielding-can edge can shorten the high-frequency current path and reduce electromagnetic leakage around the shield. Therefore, a via fence around a shielding can is generally more suitable for high-frequency shielding than a single-point ground connection. （EMI shielding + stitching vias） Faraday Cage: Why Can a Row of Ground Vias Help With Shielding? Many engineers think of the grounding vias around a PCB edge as a small Faraday cage. There is some truth to this analogy, but an important point should be noted: a PCB via fence is not an ideal, completely enclosed Faraday cage. The basic idea behind a Faraday cage is to use a continuous conductive structure to shield against electromagnetic fields through reflection, absorption, and boundary effects. On a PCB, continuous ground copper, reference planes, stitching vias, and metal shielding cans can work together to create a similar shielding structure. One important function of the grounding vias is to connect ground structures on different layers and reduce electromagnetic “openings” around the PCB edge. At high frequencies, shielding effectiveness depends on many factors, including conductor continuity, via spacing, opening size, material, operating frequency, and the overall structure. Therefore, instead of simply applying a fixed wavelength ratio, the via spacing should be determined based on the actual operating frequency, signal rise time, and PCB structure. For high-speed digital signals, the relevant frequency content is not necessarily equal to the clock frequency. Signal rise time also needs to be considered. Limitations A PCB via fence cannot completely prevent electromagnetic coupling at all frequencies. Copper and grounding vias alone have limited effectiveness against low-frequency magnetic fields. At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance, spacing, and structure of the vias can affect shielding performance. The effectiveness of the shielding structure also depends on the PCB reference planes, return paths, connectors, shielding cans, and other design elements. How Should You Design Stitching Vias Along the PCB Edge? Adding vias around the board is not simply a matter of placing them in a row. Via spacing, location, grounding method, and edge copper design all need to be considered according to the actual PCB structure. Here are some common design principles. 1. Via Spacing A common engineering approach is to estimate the via spacing based on the wavelength corresponding to the target frequency. For example, λ/10 or a smaller spacing can be used as an initial reference. However, this is not a fixed standard that applies to every PCB. Actual design should also consider: The highest frequency of interest High-speed signal rise/fall time PCB stackup Reference plane location Board-edge structure Shielding-can and connector openings For ordinary PCBs, relatively wider via spacing may be sufficient. For high-speed, RF, or high-EMI areas, the spacing may need to be reduced. Common engineering reference values include: General PCBs: approximately 50–100 mil High-speed/RF areas: approximately 30–50 mil Areas with stringent shielding requirements: further spacing reduction based on simulation or actual EMI testing Do not mechanically apply a fixed value. The final via spacing should be determined based on the actual frequency and structure. 2. Via Location Edge grounding vias should maintain an appropriate clearance from the PCB outline. Sufficient clearance should be provided according to the PCB manufacturer's fabrication capability to prevent damage to the vias during routing, milling, V-cut, or other board-edge processing. At the same time: Distribute the vias evenly along the board edge whenever possible. Avoid large gaps in the via fence. Increase via density around RF, high-speed signal, and connector areas when necessary. Connect the grounding vias to the appropriate reference ground plane rather than only to the top-layer copper. It is important to note that not every ground plane needs to be connected through the same via. The exact connection method should be determined based on the PCB stackup and return-current path. 3. Start With Continuous Ground Copper Many designers add a row of vias but overlook the ground copper between them. This alone cannot create a complete PCB ground via fence. A continuous ground copper area should be provided around the PCB edge according to the board structure, with grounding vias connecting it to the internal reference ground plane. The vias provide vertical connections, while continuous ground copper provides horizontal connections. Together, they form a more complete grounding boundary. High-speed signal traces, slots, or other structures should not arbitrarily cut through this grounding boundary. 4. Increase Via Density in Critical Areas The entire PCB does not necessarily need the same via spacing. The following areas may require additional stitching vias: Board-edge connectors and interfaces: Connectors are important paths through which external signals enter the PCB. Proper grounding vias can improve the return path around the interface and reduce edge coupling. Shielding-can areas: Dense grounding vias around the shielding-can solder pad can create a more continuous high-frequency grounding path. RF and high-speed clock areas: For areas that are particularly sensitive to EMI or crosstalk, reducing the via spacing can strengthen local shielding. Conclusion Proper stitching vias are an important part of high-speed PCB layout and PCB design .Their core function is to improve high-frequency return paths around the PCB edge and reduce electromagnetic coupling and EMI leakage through the combination of stitching vias and continuous reference-ground structures. For high-speed, RF, and EMI-sensitive PCBs, proper PCB via stitching and PCB edge shielding are particularly important. But remember: more vias are not always better, and not every PCB needs a dense row of grounding vias. Via spacing, edge clearance, reference planes, and local shielding structures should all be determined based on the actual signal frequency, rise time, and PCB stackup.
